explanation: Called cempasúchil, from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, the marigolds line paths from graves to home altars, where their colour and scent are said to lead the dead back.

claims.text: During Mexico's Day of the Dead, marigold (cempasúchil) petals are traditionally scattered in paths that are believed to guide the spirits of the dead home.
Dahlias, poinsettias and roses are not the flowers whose petals are traditionally scattered to guide spirits on the Day of the Dead.
The name cempasúchil comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.
Marigold petals are strewn along paths between graves and home altars (ofrendas), and their colour and scent are said to lead the dead back.

evidence.restatement: On the Day of the Dead, Mexican families strew orange cempasúchil marigold petals in paths meant to guide the returning dead home.
The petal-path flower is the marigold; dahlias, poinsettias (a Christmas flower) and roses are not used for those paths.
Cempasúchil comes from Nahuatl cempōhualxōchitl, 'twenty flower'; Nahuatl was the language of the Aztecs (Mexica).
